# Sport-Specific Rules

Apply these rules after the general framework.

## Cycling

- Power, normalized power, climbing load, and route repeatability matter more than raw duration alone.
- When route or segment evidence is available, explicitly analyze the route demands and the key segment outcomes instead of treating them as optional color.
- Do not treat an easy spin with low power and low HR as underperformance if the day was prescribed as recovery.
- Repeated hard cycling days with still-negative TSB should push the recommendation toward absorption or caution.

## Strength Training

- Short sessions can still be useful if the day objective was structural maintenance.
- Evaluate strength sessions by role: maintenance, activation, or main stimulus.
- Do not over-penalize low vendor training load values for strength work.

## Walking And Hiking

- Use them primarily as recovery, low-intensity aerobic support, or load accumulation depending on duration and ascent.
- A walk added on top of a hard day changes load meaningfully only when duration or terrain is substantial.

## Yoga And Mobility

- Count them as recovery-supporting work unless clearly used as additional training stress.
- Their value is often indirect: preserving movement quality and helping the next day.

## Mixed Days

- When multiple sessions happen on the same day, assess the combined day, not each session independently.
- If an athlete adds strength or yoga after a hard endurance session, preserve the main classification of the day based on the dominant stressor.

## Recovery-Sensitive Calls

- Elevated resting HR with still-negative TSB favors caution.
- Acceptable sleep alone does not justify intensity if the preceding load stack is dense.
- If physiology is sparse, anchor the decision more strongly to plan role and load sequence.
